narrative.what_i_did:
Opened with the operator's directive 'Cut the next session full of context' (the 'foul' in the literal message reads as a TTS or autocorrect substitution for 'full' given the consistent pattern of brief opening-authorization directives). Read the prior carpenter's full hand-off honest, confirmed the repo lock (stackingunderpressure/tapit-wallet matches), verified the dispatch branch (claude/multisig-orgs-status-jiLwm), and ran the four gates green before touching anything — typecheck silent, lint silent, 260 of 260 tests in 11.43 seconds, build clean with the standard file-size advisory on WalletProvider.tsx at 751 lines.

The prior session had left a five-option menu without strongly recommending one, so per PFOR-019 I surfaced the menu in chip form rather than picking unilaterally. The operator picked option (a) — the field-test polish on the VouchWitnessModal surface the prior session shipped, specifically the handshake-presence warning banner that fires when the peer has no relationship attestation for the joiner. That was the right call: the loop closes end-to-end at the substrate level after the prior two sessions, and tightening the most-recently-shipped surface while it is still fresh in mind keeps the polish honest. The cut also has a clear user-safety story — vouching warrants identity to the org, and warranting identity for someone you do not actually know is the failure mode worth surfacing explicitly rather than relying on the implicit short-pubkey-rendering tell.

The substantive shape of the cut is two small edits in VouchWitnessModal.tsx plus one paragraph in the cosigning manifest. The first edit lifts the joinerNames-lookup computation up into a named hasJoinerRelationship boolean derived from joinerNames.has(joinerKey), so the same source of truth governs both whether the display name falls back to shortKey() and whether the warning banner shows. Sharing the boolean prevents the two surfaces from ever disagreeing — if the label renders as a hex string, the banner shows; if the label renders a name, the banner does not — which removes a class of UX bugs where the two indicators could drift apart under future refactors. The second edit adds the banner itself in the review step JSX, placed between the main accent framing block and the EnvelopePreview, styled with the codebase's existing amber-banner convention (rounded-md border border-amber-200 bg-amber-50 px-3 py-2 text-xs text-amber-900) which a quick grep confirmed is the universal warning-banner styling already in use across JournalDetail, QrScanModal, MarkPresenceModal, IdentityCeremony, MembershipChainSheet, JoinOrgModal, and a dozen other surfaces. Copy reads 'You have no handshake with this person yet. Vouching means warranting their identity to the organization, so make sure you actually know who you are signing for before you sign,' framed as a personal-warning admonition rather than a hard block — the peer can still proceed if they know the person via some out-of-band channel that the wallet's holdings do not record, but they cannot proceed unwitting.

The peerNamesByPubkey aggregation gave me a moment of pause worth naming. The map populates from handshakes the peer holds AND from identity attestations the peer holds, so 'no entry for the joiner' is a slightly broader signal than 'no handshake.' If the peer happens to hold the joiner's identity attestation directly without a handshake — uncommon in practice but possible if the identity arrived via some non-handshake transport — the banner would correctly not fire because the map would have the name. Conversely, if the peer has neither a handshake nor a stored identity attestation for the joiner, the banner fires. The framing 'you have no handshake' is therefore slightly narrower than the actual condition, but it is the right framing for the user-facing copy because handshakes are the primary primitive operators recognize and it is the closest plain-English approximation. Naming the seam in the narrative so a future carpenter can see that if the wallet ever starts holding identity attestations without handshakes as a common pattern, the banner copy may need to evolve from 'no handshake' to 'no relationship attestation' or similar.

Four gates all green after: typecheck silent, lint silent, 260 of 260 tests passing in 9.92 seconds, build clean. VouchWitnessModal.tsx grew from 294 to 308 lines (14 net) — still well under the 400 soft warn. The cosigning manifest picked up one new paragraph naming this as Phase 8 Phase E4 cut 6 and recording the hasJoinerRelationship-shared-boolean shape. No other files needed to change; the cut was the smallest useful slice, exactly as the operator authorized.
narrative.whats_pending:
The vouch loop now closes end-to-end at the substrate level with the handshake-presence warning banner adding the last piece of polish on the peer-side surface. The remaining work on this loop is field-testing on real devices — the operator should be able to walk through a full vouch flow with two physical wallets, see the joiner-side progress chip tick from 0 to 1 to 2 as peer wallets respond, and see the amber banner appear on the peer side when one of the test wallets has no handshake with the joiner. If the field test surfaces UX bugs the substrate cannot have anticipated, those become the next session's input.

The four remaining options from the prior session's menu are still open. The receiveSelfMembership orgSelfDecl-lookup centralization is a small one-session cut that moves the org-declaration discovery out of HomeScreen into the receive function itself, reducing the orgDeclaration parameter useInboxAccepts has to take. It naturally pairs with moving orgDeclaration computation into useWallet, which would let both HomeScreen and useInboxAccepts pull from a single source — the same refactor seen from two angles. The JoinOrgModal proof-candidate finder extraction (findHandshakeProofCandidates and findCredentialProofCandidates plus their helpers move to src/features/connections/joinOrgProofCandidates.ts) buys roughly 50 lines of headroom on a 670-line file plus a unit-test surface that does not currently exist. The Phase D charter-amendment chain is the largest thread — multi-session, brief at project-memory/foreman-memory/projects/tapit-wallet/briefs/charter-amendment-chain-roadmap.md, and will probably reuse the receiver-aware routing pattern the vouch loop substrate uses. The appcommander metadata cleanup chip is still pending operator confirmation of whether the AppCommander cockpit polls those files from origin/main.

One small loose thread from this cut worth naming: VouchWitnessModal and CosignAsWitnessModal share roughly 80% of their post-signing scaffolding (the canonicalEnvelope textarea, the QR toggle, the copy + share + send-back buttons, the summarizePublish status rendering). A future cut when a third caller appears with the same shape — probably the Phase D charter-amendment voter surface — should pull the shared signed-envelope-return scaffolding out into a reusable primitive. Two callers do not yet justify the abstraction (especially given that the framing differences between vouch and cosign are exactly the kind of thing that would push back against a too-rigid shared component), but the seam is now visible and the next session can choose to either extract it preemptively or wait for the third caller. I lean toward waiting per the three-callers-minimum heuristic the prior session named.
narrative.what_you_could_do_better:
One honest observation. The banner copy uses the word 'handshake' as a synonym for 'relationship attestation,' but the underlying peerNamesByPubkey map populates from handshakes plus held identity attestations plus the wallet's own identity. In the common case a peer either has a handshake with the joiner or has neither — handshakes are how relationships record themselves in this codebase — so the framing reads true to operators. But if the wallet starts holding identity attestations through some non-handshake pathway as a common pattern (the journal-share workflow could in principle deposit an identity attestation without a paired handshake, for instance), the banner copy would technically still be correct but the framing 'you have no handshake' would understate what the wallet actually knows. The cleaner long-term framing is probably 'you have no recorded relationship with this person yet' or 'you have not yet acknowledged this person's identity' — but those phrasings test poorly because they are less concrete than 'handshake,' which operators recognize. I shipped with 'handshake' for the concreteness, and named the seam here so a future carpenter who notices the wallet starting to acquire identity attestations through non-handshake pathways can revisit the copy.

Nothing else surfaced beyond the declared scope this session. The cut was exactly the chunk the operator authorized — one boolean lifted, one banner added, one manifest paragraph appended — and the four gates went green on the first run after the edit. There is no half-finished thread, no surprise rework, and no late-discovered constraint.
narrative.bigger_picture:
The bigger-picture teaching of this small cut is what 'the smallest useful version correctly' looks like at the very end of a multi-session arc. The vouch loop took three sessions to land — the joiner-side fan-out and routing fix, the peer-side signing surface and useInboxAccepts extraction, and now the handshake-presence warning banner. Each cut was sized to the operator's authorization and each cut was complete in itself, but the composite is what the operator actually gets to walk through when they pick up two physical wallets and test the vouch flow end-to-end. The last cut in such an arc is often the cut that determines whether the composite feels coherent or merely functional. A vouch surface that works but lets the peer warrant an identity they do not know — without flagging that as the failure mode it is — would have shipped a mechanism rather than a trustworthy experience. The amber banner is what makes the experience trustworthy without making it paternalistic; the peer can still proceed if they know the joiner out-of-band, but they cannot proceed unwitting.

The sub-pattern this cut demonstrates is shared-source-of-truth between two surfaces that would otherwise drift. The hasJoinerRelationship boolean governs both the label fallback and the banner visibility, so they cannot disagree. The naive alternative would have been to compute the banner condition independently from the label condition — they look like the same thing, but the maintenance cost is that any future change to one has to remember to update the other. Lifting the predicate out as a named variable is a small refactor with a structural payoff: the two surfaces are now provably consistent rather than coincidentally consistent. The pattern applies broadly anywhere two pieces of UI depend on the same underlying condition — the cost of naming the predicate is one line, and the benefit is that the consistency is enforced by the type system rather than by future-carpenter vigilance.

A broader thesis-level connection: this cut closes the open seam on a primitive that, when whole, lets a community vouch for new members without any centralized arbiter. The org's join-policy gate at the receive side counts vouches against a threshold; the joiner-side fan-out scatters the request to N peers; the peer-side surface lets each peer make an individual personal-trust decision and now warns them honestly when they have no basis for that trust; the joiner-side absorb routing reassembles the vouches into a single cosigned envelope. That is a complete distributed-consent primitive built out of the same wallet.sign substrate as every other attestation in the system — no special-case cryptography, no separate transport, no organizational privilege. The same primitive that signs a journal entry signs a vouch, the same envelopeId tracks merging, the same encryptedInbox carries the return, and the same Mycelium peer network reaches the addressees. The Layer 2 inter-app signing pathway and the Layer 3 peer network are doing exactly the work they were designed to do — and the operator-facing Layer 4 surfaces are what make that work feel like a coherent product rather than a research demo. That is the thesis the Tapit Wallet exists to demonstrate, and the vouch loop is now an instance of it that operators can actually walk through and feel.

feedback_to_appcommander: Two small patterns from this cut worth noting. First, the shared-source-of-truth pattern between visual surfaces that depend on the same predicate — lifting hasJoinerRelationship out as a named boolean shared between the label fallback and the banner visibility is a one-line refactor with a structural payoff (the two surfaces cannot drift apart under future maintenance). The pattern applies broadly and is cheap to apply; probably worth a doctrine note about preferring named predicates over inline conditions when two or more JSX branches depend on the same underlying state. Second, the polish-the-fresh-surface heuristic at the end of a multi-session arc: when a substrate-level loop has just closed and the operator's authorization is open-ended ('cut the next session'), the cut that tightens the most-recently-shipped surface is usually the right call over starting a new thread, because the freshly-shipped substrate is the most likely place for a UX seam to be both visible AND fixable in a single cut. The operator picked exactly this option from the chip menu, which validates the heuristic for this style of opening-authorization session. The chip-form question pattern (PFOR-019) also worked as designed here — the operator made a one-tap decision from the iPhone rather than typing back, and the carpenter got an unambiguous direction in one round trip. Worth lifting that as a positive case study for the chip-form doctrine.
